title: Chapter 80 — The Nut
paragraphs: If, in his features, the Sperm Whale is a Sphinx, then to the phrenologist his brain looks like that geometrical circle which can never be squared.

In the full-grown creature the skull will measure at least twenty feet in length. Unhinge the lower jaw, and the side view of this skull is like the side of a moderately inclined plane resting throughout on a level base. But in life — as we have seen elsewhere — this inclined plane is filled up at an angle, and almost squared off, by the enormous mass of the junk and sperm lying on top of it. At the high end the skull forms a crater to bed that part of the mass; while under the long floor of this crater — in another cavity seldom more than ten inches long and as many deep — lies the mere handful of this monster's brain. In life the brain is at least twenty feet from his apparent forehead; it is hidden away behind its vast outworks, like the innermost citadel within the enlarged fortifications of Quebec. It is secreted in him like a choice casket, so much so that I have known some whalemen who flatly deny that the Sperm Whale has any other brain than that palpable semblance of one formed by the cubic yards of his sperm magazine. Given its strange folds, courses and convolutions, they think it more in keeping with the idea of his general might to regard that mystic part of him as the seat of his intelligence.

Plainly, then, from the phrenologist's point of view, the head of this Leviathan, while the creature is alive and whole, is a complete illusion. As for his real brain, you can neither see any sign of it then nor feel any. Like all mighty things, the whale shows a false brow to the ordinary world.

If you clear his skull of its spermy heaps and then look at its back end from behind — which is the high end — you will be struck by how much it resembles a human skull seen in the same position and from the same angle. In fact, put this reversed skull (scaled down to human size) on a plate among men's skulls, and you would unthinkingly mix it up with them; and noticing the hollows on one part of its top, you would say in phrenological terms: This man had no self-esteem and no veneration. And from those negatives, taken together with the positive fact of his enormous bulk and power, you can best form the truest, if not the most cheerful, idea of what the loftiest power is.

But if, from the comparative dimensions of the whale's actual brain, you think it incapable of being adequately charted, then I have another idea for you. If you look attentively at almost any quadruped's spine, you will be struck by the resemblance of its vertebrae to a strung necklace of dwarfed skulls, all bearing a rudimentary resemblance to the skull proper. It is a German notion that the vertebrae are absolutely undeveloped skulls. But I take it that the Germans were not the first men to perceive the curious external resemblance. A foreign friend once pointed it out to me in the skeleton of an enemy he had killed, with whose vertebrae he was inlaying the beaked prow of his canoe in a sort of bas-relief. Now, I consider that the phrenologists have left out an important thing in not pushing their investigations from the cerebellum through the spinal canal. For I believe that much of a man's character will be found indicated in his backbone. I would rather feel your spine than your skull, whoever you are. A thin joist of a spine never yet held up a full and noble soul. I rejoice in my spine, as in the firm, audacious staff of that flag which I fling half out to the world.

Apply this spinal branch of phrenology to the Sperm Whale. His skull cavity runs straight into the first neck vertebra, and in that vertebra the bottom of the spinal canal measures ten inches across and eight high, in a triangular shape with its base at the bottom. As the canal passes through the rest of the vertebrae it narrows, but for a good distance it stays very roomy. Now, naturally, this canal is filled with much the same strangely fibrous substance as the brain — the spinal cord — and connects directly with the brain. What's more, for many feet after leaving the brain's cavity, the spinal cord keeps its full thickness, nearly equal to that of the brain. Given all this, would it be unreasonable to survey and chart the whale's spine phrenologically? For seen this way, the wonderful relative smallness of his actual brain is more than made up for by the wonderful relative size of his spinal cord.

But leaving this hint to have whatever effect it may on the phrenologists, I would simply adopt the spinal theory for a moment with regard to the Sperm Whale's hump. This majestic hump, unless I am mistaken, rises over one of the larger vertebrae, and so is, in a way, its outer convex mold. Judging by its position, then, I would call this high hump the Sperm Whale's organ of firmness, or indomitableness. And you will yet have cause to learn that the great monster is indomitable.
